title: How the Ancient Greeks Interpreted Their Dreams
gist: Classicist Mirjam Kotwick argues in her new book that ancient Greek dream interpretation—from Homer through Aristotle—relied on a shared 'logic of likeness' method that continues to shape how modern language, particularly metaphor, is interpreted today.

themes.theme: Ancient dream interpretation and the roots of metaphor

insights.claim: Classicist Mirjam Kotwick's new book The Ancient Interpretation of Dreams argues that a long line of Greek thinkers—including Homer, Aeschylus, Herodotus, Plato, and Aristotle—engaged in dream interpretation using a shared method of 'reading by resemblance,' or the logic of likeness, and that this method continues to shape how figurative language is interpreted today.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Traces a specific interpretive method (resemblance-based reading) from ancient dream analysis to modern concepts like metaphor, a notable claim about the intellectual lineage of figurative-language theory.
insights.quote: a long line of Greek thinkers, including Homer, Aeschylus, Herodotus, Plato, and Aristotle, she writes, engaged in an intellectual practice of dream interpretation using a shared method—essentially reading by resemblance, or the logic of likeness—and this method continues to shape how we interpret figurative language today
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'This dream interpretation is one of the earliest recorded...'

insights.claim: In Homer's Odyssey, Penelope dreams that an eagle kills her 20 pet geese, and the eagle then explains that the geese represent her suitors and the eagle represents Odysseus, who will kill the suitors upon his return—an early recorded example of the resemblance-based dream-interpretation method Kotwick studies.
insights.speaker: Kristen French
insights.so_what: Provides the concrete textual example anchoring Kotwick's broader thesis about ancient Greek dream-interpretation methodology.
insights.quote: The geese represent her suitors, and the eagle stands in for Odysseus himself, who will kill all the suitors on his return, the bird tells her.
